title: Describe and sort quadrilaterals by sides, angles and parallel sides

lesson.title: Sorting Quadrilaterals: Sides, Angles and Parallel Lines

steps.say: You already know how to sort polygons by looking at their sides and their angles. Today we take that same skill and use it on quadrilaterals, which are just shapes with exactly four straight sides, so we can say exactly what kind of four sided shape we are looking at.

visual.caption: Four straight sides, so this is a quadrilateral

steps.say: When you meet a quadrilateral, be a detective and ask three questions. One: how long are the sides, are any of them the same? Two: what kind of corners does it have, are they square corners? Three: which sides are parallel, that means sides that run side by side like the two rails of the SkyTrain and never bump into each other.

visual.caption: Sides 8 and 3 · four square corners · two pairs of parallel sides

steps.say: Let us try it on a real one. Here is a cookie sheet shaped rectangle that is eight centimetres long and three centimetres wide. Question one, the sides: the two long sides are both eight and the two short sides are both three, so opposite sides match. Question two, the angles: all four corners are square corners. Question three: the two long sides are parallel to each other, and the two short sides are parallel to each other. Four sides, four square corners, two pairs of parallel sides. That is a rectangle.

visual.caption: Rectangle: opposite sides equal, all corners square

steps.say: Now look at this napkin. It is six centimetres by six centimetres. Run the same three checks: all four sides are six, so every side is equal. All four corners are square corners. And opposite sides are still parallel. Because all four sides are equal, we get to call it a square.

visual.caption: Square: all four sides 6 cm, all corners square

steps.say: Here is the mistake almost everybody makes. On a sorting question, when the rule says put all the rectangles in this box, lots of kids leave the square out. But look again at our six by six napkin. Does it have four sides? Yes. Four square corners? Yes. Opposite sides equal and parallel? Yes. It passes every single rectangle test, so a square is a rectangle. It is just an extra special one, because its sides are all the same. Think of it like this: a husky is a dog, even though it is a special kind of dog.

visual.caption: 5 cm by 5 cm: a square, and also a rectangle

steps.say: So sort quadrilaterals by asking those three questions every time, and remember that a shape can belong to more than one group.

lesson.answer: Check three things — sides, angles, parallel sides — and remember every square is also a rectangle.

practice.question: Ms. Yuanyuan has two placemats. The blue one is a rectangle 40 centimetres long and 25 centimetres wide. The red one has four sides that are each 30 centimetres long and four square corners. She says: put every rectangle in this basket. Which placemats go in the basket, and why?
practice.answer: Both of them. The blue one has opposite sides equal (40 and 25), four square corners and two pairs of parallel sides, so it is a rectangle. The red one is a square, but it also has four square corners with opposite sides equal and parallel, so it is a rectangle too — every square is a rectangle.
